en: The doctrine of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavāda) holds that this saṃsāra, consisting of manifold sufferings, is in every respect entirely independent of a cause;
in reality, this saṃsāra arises solely from its own intrinsic nature.

For intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is indeed independence from causes. Some things are eternally existent, some are eternally non-existent, and some are diverse; in these cases, their respective intrinsic natures are the determinants.
Water is cold on the outside, fire is hot, and likewise wind has an even touch;
by whom was this fashioned? Therefore, its establishment is due to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The occasional nature of things, however, is perceived merely through their establishment at a subsequent time;
all of this is indeed established even within the doctrine of causelessness (ahetuvāda).
In reality, however, an occasional existence is causeless,
because it is an existence, like space; for,
as far as things are concerned, their necessity is observed [only] when [a cause is present].
That too occurs solely from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
for it is precisely from intrinsic nature that existence in a restricted place and existence at a restricted time are established.
Entities arise and perish from themselves alone.
A thing that occurs only occasionally is independent of a causal complex, because it is an entity.
It would be like the category of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as accepted by the Naiyāyikas;
for if one were to admit that entities depend upon causes, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, if one accepts a succession of causes for all effects, why should God not also be accepted as such by the opponents?
Moreover, [it follows that] a jar and so forth are causeless, because they are entities.
It is like the Lord (Īśvara) and others accepted by others [as creators].
However, the causal relationship is merely conceptualized,
appearing as a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority, because things arise even from the will of a yogin.
For even in dreams and similar states, there is the production of jars and other objects;
indeed, a jar in a dream is not illusory, because it possesses substantial reality for as long as one remains in that dream until awakening.
For it is not the inherent nature of a thing that everything exists at all times; rather,
the appearance of temporal sequence— as in "the cloth arises from the threads alone"— is seen in cases such as the arising of Kṛttikā from Rohiṇī.
Even though there is an appearance of priority and posteriority, the causal relationship between those two is refuted;
for indeed, there is no basis for establishing a causal relationship in the claim that "the existent arises from the existent."
Because it is observed that a scorpion arises from cow-dung, which is of a different species,
and because the Naiyāyikas accept prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) as a cause;
sometimes a cloth [arises] from existing threads.
Sometimes, because curd is seen arising from milk that has perished,
the fact that [an effect] occurs in a restricted place and the fact that it occurs at a restricted time are themselves causes residing in the very nature [of the cause].
But this is not the case when one accepts the relationship of cause and effect;
for it is by their very nature that cloth and other such effects reside in the location of the threads, and not in the location of the shuttle and other such implements.
Thus, it ultimately follows that even occasional occurrence arises from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone;
for even if an effect were causeless, its occurrence at a specific subsequent time would still be restricted by what is considered its respective cause.
However, the restriction that [an entity] does not persist through another time is also established by its very nature;
for the world does not proceed with a specific purpose in mind.
The restriction acts like adamantine glue,
by which the agency of any conscious being would be established.
This would be so if activity were necessarily pervaded by having a purpose;
however, it is not thus,
because we observe activity even in spontaneous actions where no purpose is consciously intended.

Furthermore, in the absence of those who perform useless actions, even the prohibitory statement of the authors of the *Dharma-sūtras*— that "one should not perform useless action"— would become devoid of scope. For indeed, an activity characterized by inhalation and exhalation is observed to have a purpose.
It occurs precisely without any further deliberation;
otherwise, there would be no death for any living being whatsoever.

Just as weeping occurs when suffering is intense, laughter, singing, and so forth occur when happiness is intense, even without reference to any specific purpose; this is established by universal experience.
Activity, however, necessarily has a purpose. Therefore:
"How can there be the production of the world from Brahman, who is devoid of purpose?
To this, the venerable teachers say: "Just as inhalation, exhalation, and so forth occur by their very nature without aiming at any external purpose,"

In this way, even for Īśvara, there will be an activity in the form of sport (*līlā*) arising solely from his own nature (*svabhāva*), without depending on any subsequent purpose; and "nature cannot be questioned. To this, I say: if even Īśvara is dependent upon nature, then [the same applies] in the Śaṅkara system as well.
If he will bring about creation after having willed it,
then let it be considered that creation proceeds from nature (svabhāva) alone, without a cause.
What is the use of this useless appendage, a God?
Even though Praśastapāda beats the drum for the doctrine of God, how can creation come about through a God whose desires are already fulfilled? Such is the doubt.

For the sake of providing an answer, one must take refuge in the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) alone; or else, [the Lord's] activity proceeds from the very nature of His power (*śaktisvabhāvyāt*),
just as, by intrinsic nature, the seasonal succession of spring and so forth brings about the production of transformations in both the stationary and moving worlds.
Likewise, when the powers of manifestation, grace, and withdrawal belonging to God are manifested in succession, they serve as the causes for the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of living beings.
If God’s status as God were rooted solely in his own nature (*svabhāva*), then what would be the purpose of postulating a God?
Furthermore, God is not the cause,
because, despite meeting the conditions for perception, he is not perceived.
Like the horn of a hare;
for the horn of a hare has no perceivable existence.
Therefore, there is no cause for entities.
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because no cause is perceived for such things as the filaments of a lotus or the sharpness of thorns.
And just as external objects are causeless because no cause for them can be apprehended, so too are internal phenomena such as suffering and the like.
It is precisely the state of being causeless.
Here too, the formulation of the inference is as follows:
whatever is occasional is causeless.
Just as the sharpness of a thorn and so forth [are causeless],
and since suffering and other such things occur only occasionally, they too must be entirely without cause.
Therefore, it was said by Śāntarakṣita:
"In their arising, entities have no dependence on themselves or on another;
for all entities indeed come into being independent of any cause."
Who indeed creates the variegation of the lotus filaments and other parts? By whom was the peacock’s eye-pattern and such variegated forms fashioned?
Just as the sharpness of thorns and the like is without cause, so too is this.
Because they occur only occasionally, suffering and the like likewise lack a cause.
This is a negation of their being causes, nor is it an affirmation of something indescribable;
it is not a description of an intrinsic nature, because there is a necessity regarding the limit [of their occurrence].
